items.tx:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. 

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

History was made last night. For months, we were saying that 2026 was the most consequential midterm election of our lifetimes. Unfortunately, we were right. S
items.tx:
History was made last night.

For months, we were saying that 2026 was the most consequential midterm election of our lifetimes. 

Unfortunately, we were right. Sometimes history is to be celebrated; other times, it is to be mourned. Always, it must be reckoned with.

2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an ass kicking. It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation. What happened, and why? What are the consequences, and where on earth do we go from here?

When all the votes were counted, the problem wasn’t turnout. Instead, our voters, Republicans, Libertarians, Independents, showed up and voted, and rejected our candidates, voting Democrat instead. We’ve lost the House. We’ve lost the Senate. When all is said and done, we will have lost eight to 10 Senate seats.

We lost in historically red states, like South Carolina and North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa. We lost in purple states, like Michigan, and New Hampshire, and Georgia. And we just barely won by just a single point in bright red states like Florida and Louisiana, and then there’s Texas.

Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas. In the Lone Star State, we lost every single statewide election. For weeks, I had been publicly warning on this podcast that we were in very real danger of losing everything in Texas. Far too few believed that was possible. I am very, very sorry that it came to pass. Texas has not had a Democrat governor since 1994. We haven’t had a Democrat senator since 1993. Now we’ll have both.

Why were the results so overwhelming? Pundits and analysts will break down the results for weeks or months or even years to come, but several things are already evident today.

Years ago, the very best political advice I ever got was from Heidi. She said, “It’s not about you. It’s about them. It’s about their kids, their families, their hopes, their dreams, their futures.” Too many politicians forget that.

Take the state of Kansas, for example, a state that has not elected a Democrat senator since 1932. It just did. Here’s what exit polling showed were the top issues in Kansas.

Number one, cost of living, energy, and groceries. That was listed as number one by 30.6 percent of voters. 
Corruption. Number two, 18.5%. 
The cost of the Iran war, 10.1%. 
The candidates are terrible, 7.9%. 
The Canada trade war, 7.6%. 
The GOP didn’t do enough to support Trump, 6.6%. 
Republicans didn’t pass the Save America Act, 5.6%. 
Trump’s focus on monuments, 5.5%, and data centers and AI, 3.8%.

The top issue, cost of living, is very real. Too many in politics dismissed it. They didn’t understand. They pointed to the macro numbers showing the stock markets soaring, median income at record highs, and poverty at record lows. Those data are true, but they don’t tell all of the story.

Here are some stats that are a lot more real and personal. Spam, Hormel’s processed meat substitute, broke record sales, selling 113 million cans last year. That is nearly as much spam as was sold during the entirety of World War II. 29 percent of Americans have used buy now, pay later for groceries this year. That’s double the share just two years ago.

In August, banks repossessed 42% more homes than they did last year. In 2024, car repossessions topped 2.3 million, above the 2009 peak in the middle of the Great Financial Crisis. In 2025, 6% of 401k holders took hardship withdrawals, paying penalties. That is a record, and triple the norm.

And here’s one that’s really stunning. Americans made more than 75 million paid plasma donations in 2026. That’s another record. That means 200,000 Americans every single day, with a needle in their arm, just to pay for groceries.

That is very real pain from real Americans, and too many Republican politicians seem like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care. Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high.

Tariffs have made eve

🚨🇺🇸 From Melania stopping the immigration crackdown to advisers warning the Iran war would cost the midterms, here’s what really happened inside the White House before Tuesday’s disaster...

The first lady's complaints led the president to tell aides that Stephen Miller had "gone too far," and that was just one of the decisions the Journal traces.

Other details from inside the White House:

-Advisers warned him in the spring the Iran war could cost the midterms; he said there was "plenty of time," and privately asked even junior staffers at photo ops whether he should change course

-Told aides polls on affordability were "fake," and reminded them he won 2016 without commissioning any

-Said at times he "didn't care about the midterms at all" and was tired of domestic issues he saw as smaller than foreign policy and his legacy

-Thune got off the phone six times believing he'd talked Trump out of endorsing Paxton; Trump backed him anyway, then complained about his candidacy

-Trump pushed stronger Republican candidates out of Senate races in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Texas; Democrats won all four

-Brian Kemp turned down a Senate run after Trump called him "disloyal" at a rally

-Cabinet officials told oil executives in March the war would end by April; Trump was "shocked" to learn the military was short on munitions and cut a Russian fuel deal to get prices down

-Focus groups kept bringing up the ballroom and the arch unprompted: "It seems like he wants to put his name on everything"

Advisers warned about the war, the polls warned about prices, and focus groups kept bringing up the ballroom... but the final speech before the election was about algae in the Reflecting Pool.

For a party now facing a Democratic House and Senate, the lesson is pretty simple: next time someone says “plenty of time,” check the calendar...

items.t: A 77-year-old King, still in cancer treatment, flew nine days through a region that has spent the year telling him it wants to leave. He stood in a tropical do
items.tx:
A 77-year-old King, still in cancer treatment, flew nine days through a region that has spent the year telling him it wants to leave. He stood in a tropical downpour without an umbrella. He went to the one republic whose president had publicly told him to apologise. And he came home with 56 countries agreeing to double their trade with each other by 2030. That is soft power. Nobody else alive can do it.

The Bahamas first. He hadn’t been back in 53 years, not since he stood in for his mother at independence in 1973. He got off the plane and said “I’ve arrived, thank God!” in Bahamian dialect, and that was the tour decided. Danced at Junkanoo. Sat with a youth rally at Clifford Park. Waded about in the mangroves at Bonefish Pond talking coastal resilience with people whose homes depend on it.

Then Guyana. A republic since 1970. President Ali had said out loud that the King should apologise, and the King went anyway. Met him at State House, laid a wreath, sat with the Toshaos, the elected leaders of the Indigenous villages, 26 years after he first walked into the Iwokrama rainforest and became its patron. His Foundation is now drawing up Georgetown’s urban plan with the government. You don’t get asked to do that by a country that resents you.

Then Antigua and Barbuda. The first Head of the Commonwealth ever to set foot there. At the Independence parade the sky opened, Camilla made off under the only umbrella in the stadium and the King stood in the rain miming one until somebody found him his own, laughing. The clip went round the world and did more for the monarchy than a thousand press releases.

Then he gave the speech people said he’d dodge. He didn’t. The slave trade “still casts a shadow” over these islands, he said, and the history fills him with horror and profound personal sorrow. He said the Commonwealth is “a response to the world of today.” Then he got out of the way and let the leaders work.

And they worked. Smallest host nation in Commonwealth history. 3,000 delegates in a country of 100,000 people. $52 billion of bankable projects on the table across 28 countries. Half a billion dollars of new money. A $300 million fund to put skills into 10 million young people. A trade portal, a trade target, a debt agenda the UK will carry into its G20 presidency. And on reparations, the thing everyone said would blow it up, Britain agreed to a structured, time-bound dialogue and Gaston Browne said it would not divide the Commonwealth. It didn’t.

No treaty makes any of these countries turn up. They turn up. 56 nations, 2.7 billion people, a third of humanity, and the one thing they have in common is a man who flies in, listens, gets rained on, and asks for nothing.

A word for Shirley Botchwey too. Her first CHOGM as Secretary-General. First African woman to run the Secretariat, second African after Nigeria’s own Chief Emeka Anyaoku. She promised a summit of ambition and action and then did something nobody had done in 28 of these meetings: she put investors in the room with the heads of government. Ghana should be proud of her. Africa is.

People keep asking what a monarchy is for in 2026. This week was the answer. Not power. Presence.

Well done, Antigua. God Save The King.

@RoyalFamily @commonwealthsec #CHOGM2026

The Democrats may have taken control of the House and the Senate, they may have humiliated Donald Trump and the Republican Party, but the real fight is only beginning. It is not simply a battle to hold the corrupt Trump regime to account, something that can only be done if the Democrats are willing overcome their reluctance to carry out impeachment proceedings against the president. It is also a battle to sweep away the corporate-indentured hierarchy of the Democratic Party, including Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries.

The Democratic Party since the presidency of Bill Clinton, who gave us the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), the greatest betrayal of the working class since the 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, and gutted New Deal-era welfare programs such as the Aid to Families with Dependent Children, is a more polished version of corporate and oligarchic rule, abjectly subservient to the war machine, the Israel lobby and their funders in the billionaire class.

The country is broken. Corruption, in both parties, is endemic. Federal agencies have been hollowed out and destroyed. The courts, including the Supreme Court, have been handed over to right-wing ideologues. The working class is crippled with debt peonage and substandard wages. Constitutional norms and protections have been erased. Billionaires, including Trump, pay little to no income tax. The 2010 Citizens United Supreme Court ruling, which allows big business to fund their hand-picked candidates, sustains a system of legalized bribery.

The public may clamor for a raise in the minimum wage, Medicare for All, regulation of the big banks and private equity firms, an end to arms shipments to Israel and campaign finance reform, but no one in the leadership of the Democratic Party listens or cares. They serve their paymasters.

Will cutthroat capitalism, sold to us under the sanitized name of neoliberalism, be allowed to continue to impoverish the citizenry and funnel wealth upwards into the hands of the 1 percent? Will corporations be regulated and policed? Will corporate criminals be brought to trial? Will our democracy be restored? Or will the grotesque sight of a trillionaire, Elon Musk, gutting federal agencies and pouring hundreds of millions into elections to try and control the outcome be normalized?

The handful of politicians who attempt to confront the corruption and the devastation visited on the American working class through deindustrialization and deregulation, such as Bernie Sanders, see their campaigns sabotaged by the Democratic Party leadership, including Barack Obama.

We must demand that progressive candidates, including Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson, build coalitions to oust the Democratic Party leadership, raise the minimum wage, enact universal health care, prosecute corporate crime and impeach Trump. It will be up to us.

Of course, this fight will mean not only jettisoning a corrupt Democratic Party leadership, but turning on the mega-donors, lobbyists and corporations that fund and control the Democratic Party.

The effort to wrest the party back from the hands of corporations and oligarchs will be vicious and difficult. It will require us to rely on the power of mass movements to sever these bonds. Nothing else will work.

If we fail, our anemic democracy will not be saved by these midterm elections, but doomed.

items.t: Some of my immediate takeaways from the midterms: 1. This wasn’t a blue wave. This wasn’t even a blue tsunami. This was a blue mass extinction event. The Repub
items.tx:
Some of my immediate takeaways from the midterms:

1. This wasn’t a blue wave. This wasn’t even a blue tsunami. This was a blue mass extinction event. The Republican coalition which seemingly gave Trump a mandate 2 years ago fell apart everywhere, on all sides. There was a big polling error, but what happened is that polls underestimated Democrats. The generic ballot will seemingly end at D+13. This goes above and beyond what the rosiest Dem forecasts thought could happen. 
2. Trumpism has been conclusively smashed at the polls, not even just Trump himself. The Rust Belt didn’t have any sympathy for tariffs, hawkish voters had no sympathy for the Iran War, and non-college educated whites had no sympathy for the attacks on colleges and mass ICE raids. Republicans might’ve lost young men for a generation. All types of Republicans across the country faced the wrath of voters. The GOP has been completely transformed into MAGA’s fashion, but that will be a detriment for voters. Turns out, Trump only broke the laws of political gravity when he had the benefit of the doubt regarding a (relatively) peaceful world and a good economy. 
3. Zohran Mamdani is the most influential Dem politician of the decade already. His message, though very much altered for different states and different candidates, became the Democratic Party’s midterm platform. The idea that Mamdani would be some fringe figure in the Dem coalition, as proffered by some pundits last year, has been thoroughly disproven. He will be only next to Obama and Bernie as the models for all Dem politicians, particularly on the left, going forward
4. Israel took a drubbing at the polls. The Iran War created the high gas prices and inflation that drew the floor out from underneath the GOP coalition. We already know how Dem voters view Israel as being the worst thing on Earth. But now Republicans (even JD Vance as we’ve seen today) are also mad at Israel for pushing them into a war that’s remarkably unpopular, and that America will ultimately lose. The GOP will continue to be institutionally pro-Israel, due to donors and other factors, but GOP politicians and particularly pollsters now view Israel as a liability, both personally and politically. 
5. The effect on the 2028 Dem primary sweepstakes is as such: Josh Shapiro’s case is over (why would Dems care about nominating an electorally skillful moderate after THIS kind of anti-GOP drubbing?), Gavin Newsom might now just become irrelevant, and the stock of such characters as Mark Kelly, Ro Khanna, Andy Beshear, Elissa Slotkin, Cory Booker, Jared Polis, Gretchen Whitmer, and Pete Buttigieg has gone down (Chris Murphy’s stock has also gone down too, for other reasons). Kamala Harris’ stock has gone up, as Dems now begin to feel that Kamala’s loss has been properly avenged and she can now start planning her reconquest. James Talarico is ascendant (Beto had a serious 2020 campaign just by *barely losing* a Texas senate seat, and a Dem Texas Governor removes the issue of losing his senate seat to the GOP), and AOC had her best night possible. Primary voters will now care less about electability, and care more about totally repudiating Trumpism and policy. Those are the lanes progressives do best in. AOC, even she prefers to become a Senator, is now positioned to be the Barry Goldwater or even Ronald Reagan of the Dem left. But the best night goes to Jon Ossoff. 18 point victory in a swing state. He is now the frontrunner, no ifs or buts.

items.tx:
I just spoke to @VDHanson about what the midterm results mean for Trump, the Republican Party, MAGA, and 2028.

Here’s what he told me:

The Republican losses were predictable. Since 1900 the White House party has lost House seats in ~90% of midterms (Senate in ~75%). The size of this wave (dozens in House, 7-9 Senate) is the real outlier.

Trump has roughly 70 days to lock in judges, cabinet picks, and nominees before the new Congress arrives.

With a ~45-seat Republican Senate, Trump will have to keep all Republicans in line or face a “veto-proof” Democratic Congress.

Trump can and will act unilaterally on foreign policy and executive orders. Historical precedent is clear. “The imperial presidency operates as they wish,” Hanson says.

The “affordability” story was heavily media-driven. Inflation is roughly one-third of 2022’s 9.1%. Family income is up ~$14k, GDP is stronger, stocks are +20k, poverty is down. The real issue is the 21% cumulative price jump he inherited—and the administration never clearly explained how slower inflation + higher incomes fixes it.

Trump never explained in full why the Iran campaign was necessary. The first 38 days were a historic success; stopping short and endless talk of negotiations let Iran claim they stopped him. The messaging, not the campaign itself, was the biggest problem.

Unlike this Congress, the new Democratic majority will have iron party discipline. That contrast will matter.

2028 starts now. The Vance-Rubio pairing will face immediate pressure—many will want Rubio at the top of the ticket, but Vance can’t run as VP again. Democrats will jump in fast. Their nominee will almost certainly come from the left of the party.

The Republican path to recovery, Hanson argues, runs through results, not rhetoric. A strong economy in 2026-27, a finished Iran campaign, and visible progress on affordability give the next nominee a real chance. Without those, the structural advantages of the new Democratic Congress become decisive.

In 2018, Brian Kemp ran for governor of Georgia. He was also the man running the election.
As Secretary of State, his office had canceled nearly 670,000 voter registrations in 2017 alone. Then, weeks before Election Day, it froze 53,000 more under a rule called "exact match." A missing hyphen. A dropped initial. That was enough. Nearly 70% of those frozen applications belonged to Black Georgians, in a state that's about 32% Black.
Stacey Abrams lost by about 55,000 votes.
She didn't wait for the next race. She built Fair Fight and went to work in every one of Georgia's 159 counties. She recruited poll watchers, ran registration drives, and took the system to court.
Georgia organizers registered more than 800,000 new voters.
Two years later, Georgia went blue for president for the first time since 1992. Two months after that, it sent two Democrats to the U.S. Senate and handed them control of the chamber.

Last night Jon Ossoff won re-election. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Democrat elected governor of Georgia since 1998. Tanya Miller became the state's first woman attorney general.

items.t: When Keisha Lance Bottoms was 8, she used to come home from school and find her father making dinner. Major Lance was a soul singer who sung “The Monkey Time”
items.tx:
When Keisha Lance Bottoms was 8, she used to come home from school and find her father making dinner. Major Lance was a soul singer who sung “The Monkey Time” and opened for the Beatles.

One afternoon, Keisha found police officers in the house. Her father was in handcuffs. “Babies, it’s going to be OK,” he told his children as the officers took him away. “I will be back.” The police told Keisha to sit on the sofa, and she was so afraid of getting in trouble that she stayed there until her mother came home. 

Her parents divorced while her father was in prison. Her mother, Sylvia, worked several jobs, and the ballet lessons Keisha had taken were suddenly more than the family could afford. When Keisha talked about her daddy in those years, she kept it simple. Her dad was living in Columbus, she would say. Then he was living in Jackson, or Eatonton. Those were the towns where he was being held. 

Isitoshe, 

Major Lance died suddenly at 55, the year his daughter finished law school. She was 24 and thought 55 sounded old. As she approached that age herself, with four children of her own, it struck her how young he had been. She knew what it was to come home one day and find your father being taken away. Now she thought about her children waking up one morning and finding her gone. 

Becoming their mother had taken years. Keisha had severe fibroids, went through failed rounds of IVF and underwent what she remembers as more than a dozen surgeries, including a partial hysterectomy. When her husband, Derek, suggested adoption, she worried that saying yes meant she had given up on what she had been asking God for. They went ahead with the interviews, the home visits and the paperwork. Then, in 2002, while they were away on a cruise, word came that a six-month-old boy was available for adoption. 

Sylvia spoke to the caseworker. “Hold that baby!” she writes in her book. Keisha and Derek brought Lance home. In time, they adopted Langston and then the twins, Lennox and Lincoln. 

Yesterday, Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms governor. She became the first Black woman elected to lead a U.S. state. 

May the day break

qt.t:
He’s walking through a neighborhood and the people don’t run. They don’t look away. They call him “Don Pablo” with real warmth. Some smile. Some thank him. One moment even references the generosity he’s known for in these streets.

This is the other side of the myth, the carefully built public image. While the world saw a ruthless drug lord, certain communities saw a man who built houses, handed out money, and filled the space the government left empty.

The camera doesn’t need to explain the contradiction. It’s right there in the greetings, the gratitude, and the quiet respect.

Monster to some. Benefactor to others.
And in places like this, both versions of him were true at the same time.

items.tx:
A fresh political challenge is emerging for President Donald Trump's administration, this time from within the Republican Party.

Republican Congressman Thomas Massie says he plans to force a House vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as early as next week, unless Hegseth resigns.

The move comes amid growing criticism of Hegseth's handling of the Iran war and the political fallout from Republicans' losses in the 2026 midterm elections.

Massie previously introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of exceeding his constitutional authority and violating laws governing military operations.

While Trump continues to defend his Defense Secretary, the impeachment push raises questions about divisions within the Republican Party and who should bear responsibility for the administration's military decisions.

Could Hegseth become the first major casualty of the Republicans' midterm defeat, or will Trump's continued support be enough to keep him in office?
